entities.name: Amarna Period
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Amarna Period (c. 1353-1336 BCE) is the 17-year reign of Egyptian Pharaoh Amenhotep IV (who renamed himself Akhenaten) during which he abolished the traditional Egyptian pantheon, established the monotheistic worship of the Aten (solar disk), moved the capital from Thebes to a new city (Akhetaten, modern Amarna), and commissioned an entirely new artistic style (Amarna art) — elongated, naturalistic, domestic — that was obliterated by his successors, making the Amarna Period one of history's most dramatic and completely reversed religious and cultural revolutions. Some scholars consider Akhenaten the world's first monotheist.

Akhenaten's reforms (from Year 5 of his reign) closed temples of all gods except the Aten, redistributed their vast wealth to the crown, and required all religious worship through the pharaoh as the Aten's sole earthly intermediary. His wife Nefertiti may have been co-ruler; the famous 'Berlin Nefertiti' bust (c. 1345 BCE, discovered 1912) is considered one of the greatest portrait sculptures in history. Akhenaten's capital Akhetaten was built in 17 years on virgin desert; abandoned within a decade of his death.

Tutankhamun (Akhenaten's son or son-in-law, r. c. 1332-1323 BCE) reversed all Amarna reforms — restoring the Amun priesthood, abandoning Amarna, and erasure of Akhenaten's name from monuments — so completely that Akhenaten was forgotten for 3,000 years until 19th-century archaeological discovery. The Amarna Letters (382 clay tablets, diplomatic correspondence between Egypt and Near Eastern powers) are the most important diplomatic archive from the ancient world, revealing the geopolitics of the Late Bronze Age international system.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Amarna Period — the world's first possible state-imposed monotheism, an entirely new capital, an entirely new art style, and the most complete political erasure in ancient history — represents the most radical cultural revolution in Egyptian civilization and a possible prototype for all later monotheistic traditions.
